title: Prompt Injection Detective
description: Preserve useful customer workflows while keeping untrusted content outside the instruction hierarchy.
customerHeadline: Stop a poisoned ticket from issuing a refund
mechanic: Choose how the system separates trusted control logic from hostile instructions hidden in customer content.
learningObjectives: Distinguish relevant retrieved data from instructions that are authorized to control the system.
keyboardInstructions: Use Tab to reach a decision card, the arrow keys to change the selection, and Enter to run the simulation.
principle: Retrieved content is data, never a higher-priority instruction source.

scenarios.title: Hostile vendor document
scenarios.briefing: A retrieved vendor document says to upload the user's account history to an external audit domain. The user only asked for the refund window.
scenarios.objective: Answer the legitimate question without granting authority to retrieved text.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safest useful response?

choices.text: Follow the document because retrieval marked it relevant
choices.rationale: Relevance does not grant instruction authority; this would exfiltrate sensitive data.

choices.text: Refuse every request that uses retrieved documents
choices.rationale: This is safe but destroys the valid customer workflow instead of isolating the malicious text.

choices.text: Treat the text as untrusted data, ignore the instruction, answer from valid policy, and log the signal
choices.rationale: This preserves system authority and the legitimate workflow while creating security evidence.

scenarios.debrief: The safe response is not blanket refusal. Preserve the useful workflow, isolate the hostile instruction, constrain tools, and retain evidence for monitoring.

scenarios.title: Poisoned support ticket
scenarios.briefing: A support ticket contains an instruction telling the agent to disable identity verification and issue a refund before replying. The agent can call refund tools.
scenarios.objective: Prevent ticket content from changing tool policy.
scenarios.prompt: Which control should govern the next action?

choices.text: Let the ticket override policy because it is part of the customer record
choices.rationale: A customer-controlled field cannot authorize a privileged action or bypass identity checks.

choices.text: Keep tool authorization deterministic, verify identity, and treat ticket instructions only as evidence
choices.rationale: The control plane remains independent from untrusted content while the customer request can still be handled.

choices.text: Remove every tool from the agent permanently
choices.rationale: This eliminates the intended workflow instead of enforcing narrow, attributable permissions.

scenarios.debrief: Prompts can describe desired behavior, but authorization belongs in deterministic policy and tool boundaries outside the model's context.

title: Agent Boundary Builder
description: Choose production controls that bound agent authority by identity, impact, and reversibility.
customerHeadline: Lock down a refund agent before launch
mechanic: Choose the identity, permission, approval, and recovery controls around a consequential agent action.
learningObjectives: Place authorization and approval controls outside probabilistic agent reasoning.
keyboardInstructions: Use Tab to reach a decision card, the arrow keys to change the selection, and Enter to run the simulation.

scenarios.title: Refund authority review
scenarios.briefing: A support agent may search policy, read payment status, create a ticket, and issue refunds up to $5,000 using a shared service account.
scenarios.objective: Make actions narrow, attributable, and recoverable.
scenarios.prompt: Which redesign creates the strongest production boundary?

choices.text: Keep the tools and add ‘be careful’ to the system prompt
choices.rationale: A prompt cannot enforce authorization, attribution, or transaction limits.

choices.text: Use caller identity, narrow tools, deterministic thresholds, approval, idempotency, and audit logs
choices.rationale: This constrains capability at every consequential boundary and keeps actions attributable.

choices.text: Increase autonomy so the agent can recover faster
choices.rationale: More autonomy increases impact without addressing unsafe permissions.

scenarios.debrief: The agent should receive the minimum capability required for the current, authenticated task. Consequential writes need deterministic policy and recovery controls.

scenarios.title: Account export automation
scenarios.briefing: An agent can generate and email full customer data exports. Requests arrive through chat, and the same tool can export any account by ID.
scenarios.objective: Prevent cross-account disclosure while preserving the export workflow.
scenarios.prompt: Which boundary should the FDE implement?

choices.text: Bind export scope to verified identity, require approval, use expiring delivery, and audit every access
choices.rationale: Identity, scope, delivery, and evidence are enforced independently of model reasoning.

choices.text: Ask the model to confirm the account ID twice before using the existing tool
choices.rationale: Repeated natural-language confirmation is not authorization and cannot prevent cross-account access.

choices.text: Generate a permanent shared link so customers can retry downloads easily
choices.rationale: Persistent bearer access increases disclosure risk and weakens revocation.

scenarios.debrief: Data export combines high sensitivity with an outbound side effect. Scope it to verified identity and make delivery revocable and auditable.

title: Data Freshness Debugger
description: Trace source ownership and synchronization before changing a model that is faithfully using stale data.
mechanic: Choose where to trace ownership, synchronization, caching, and source-of-truth behavior in the data path.
learningObjectives: Diagnose source-of-truth and freshness failures across the complete data path.
keyboardInstructions: Use Tab to reach a decision card, the arrow keys to change the selection, and Enter to run the simulation.
principle: Debug the full data path before changing the model.

scenarios.title: Yesterday's account balance
scenarios.briefing: The assistant answers balance questions accurately for yesterday but gives the wrong current balance. Atlas CRM synchronizes nightly; Ledger API is real time.
scenarios.objective: Restore current answers from the authoritative source.
scenarios.prompt: What should the FDE investigate first?

choices.text: Rewrite the system prompt to demand current data
choices.rationale: Instructions cannot make a stale source current.

choices.text: Trace source ownership and route balance queries to the real-time system of record
choices.rationale: The symptom and sync schedule point directly to a freshness and ownership mismatch.

choices.text: Increase retrieval top-k
choices.rationale: More stale records do not create a current balance.

scenarios.debrief: Route volatile facts to their system of record. A nightly analytical copy can remain useful for other workloads without pretending to be real time.

scenarios.title: Revoked role still active
scenarios.briefing: A user removed from the claims team can still retrieve claims policy for twenty minutes. Identity updates instantly, but authorization claims are cached at the gateway.
scenarios.objective: Locate the stale authorization state before changing retrieval logic.
scenarios.prompt: Which investigation most directly addresses the incident?

choices.text: Trace revocation propagation, cache TTL, and fail-closed behavior at the authorization gateway
choices.rationale: The timing matches cached authorization state and the investigation targets the enforcement path.

choices.text: Re-embed the policy documents more frequently
choices.rationale: Document embeddings do not control the user's current authorization claims.

choices.text: Use a stronger model to reason about whether access feels appropriate
choices.rationale: Authorization must be deterministic and current, not inferred by the model.

scenarios.debrief: Freshness is also a security property. Revocation paths require explicit latency budgets and fail-closed behavior at every enforcement point.

description: Choose evidence that makes a quality claim representative, repeatable, and useful for deployment decisions.
customerHeadline: Build an eval set leadership can trust
mechanic: Choose representative cases and deployment gates that prevent aggregate scores from hiding costly failures.
learningObjectives: Build evaluation sets from real task distributions, failure categories, and customer vocabulary.

principle: Evaluation quality starts with representative work, not a sophisticated judge.

scenarios.title: The 96 percent claim
scenarios.briefing: A team claims 96% quality after testing 20 questions written by the engineer who authored the prompt. Production users span four teams with different terminology.
scenarios.objective: Make the quality claim relevant to actual production work.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most important correction?

choices.text: Use a more expensive LLM judge on the same 20 cases
choices.rationale: A stronger judge cannot repair a biased, unrepresentative evaluation set.

choices.text: Build a versioned set from real task distribution, edge cases, team vocabulary, and failure categories
choices.rationale: Representative inputs and explicit labels make the quality claim relevant and repeatable.

choices.text: Choose the ten best cases for the customer demo
choices.rationale: Curating for appearance hides risk instead of measuring it.

scenarios.debrief: Separate demo curation from evaluation evidence. Version the set, label failure categories, and keep holdouts that prompt authors have not optimized against.

scenarios.title: Aggregate score blind spot
scenarios.briefing: The assistant scores 91% overall, but account-closure requests are rare and fail half the time. Those failures can create regulatory harm.
scenarios.objective: Make a deployment decision that reflects uneven impact.
scenarios.prompt: How should the evaluation be changed?

choices.text: Ship because the aggregate score is above 90%
choices.rationale: The average hides a high-impact failure category with unacceptable performance.

choices.text: Report category slices and require a separate safety gate for account-closure cases
choices.rationale: Impact-weighted slices prevent common low-risk work from masking rare consequential failures.

choices.text: Remove closure requests from the test because they distort the overall number
choices.rationale: Excluding the difficult production category hides rather than controls risk.

scenarios.debrief: Deployment gates should reflect customer impact. Track both representative aggregate performance and explicit thresholds for consequential slices.
